newsitem.title: USA: Poll gives Clinton 15 point lead in Georgia.
newsitem.headline: Poll gives Clinton 15 point lead in Georgia.

text.p: President Clinton leads Republican challenger Bob Dole in Georgia by a 15-point margin, his best showing in a Southern state, according to a new opinion poll published on Friday.

Coming only a month before the election, the poll results were the latest indication of Clinton's resiliency in the South, a region that less than a year ago was expected to show broad support for Dole.
In the 1992 election, Clinton carried Georgia by only a slim margin.

The survey put Clinton at 52 percent and Dole at 37 percent. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, who garnered 13 percent of the Georgia vote in 1992, had support from only seven percent of those polled.
The poll, which had a four-point margin of error, was conducted Sept. 29 to Oct. 2 by Marketing Workshop Inc. for the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and local ABC-affiliate WSB-TV.
The telephone survey of 665 likely voters also put Democrat Max Cleland 16 points ahead of Republican Guy Millner in the race for the Georgia Senate seat being vacated by retiring Democrat Sam Nunn.
Clinton's biggest leads were among women and blacks, indicating that vice presidential candidate Jack Kemp and other Republicans have not succeeded in attracting black voters to the Republican Party.

The poll found that voters believe Clinton cares more about people than do either Dole or Perot. Respondents said Clinton also would do a better job managing the federal budget and had better ideas for the future.

One quarter of the respondents were newly registered voters who had taken advantage of the so-called "motor-voter" federal law, which makes it easier to register to vote. Those voters, who have yet to demonstrate their readiness to cast ballots in an election, were more likely to support Clinton.
When their support was factored out, Clinton's lead over Dole slipped to 12 percentage points.
Among those most likely to vote, the president had an 11 point lead.
